title: With Due Respect (Vol. 4) -- Ch. 2: Suppressing Neri's Testimony
keywords: a nebulous claim of executive privilege
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4) -- CJP's November 25, 2007 Inquirer column on the Palace's attempt to suppress former NEDA chief Romulo Neri's Senate testimony in the $329-million national broadband network (NBN) scandal by a 'nebulous claim of executive privilege'

His assessment that Malacañang has little chance in court -- measured against the parameters of executive privilege set in Senate v. Ermita (April 20, 2006) -- because it had neither shown a 'superior public interest' for secrecy nor followed the required process

A primer on the six parameters of executive privilege from Philippine jurisprudence: Congress's right to information, the three categories of withholdable information, 'disclosure is the rule and secrecy the exception,' that only the President may invoke it, that it covers information (not officials), and that disputes are for the Supreme Court to judge

His sharper political point about the 'Palace strategy' of muddling issues, delaying resolution and tiptoeing 'from crisis to crisis' -- a strategy that, lamentably, had worked amid insufficient public outrage ('Kawawa naman tayong mga Pinoy!')
sub_topics: The snub: Romulo Neri skipped the Senate hearing on the $329-million NBN project, with Executive Secretary Ermita justifying his absence by a 'nebulous claim of executive privilege'

What Neri had revealed: he testified that resigned Comelec Chair Benjamin Abalos offered him a P200-million bribe ('Sec, may 200 ka dito'), but 'clammed up' on President Arroyo's involvement, asserting executive privilege

The Palace dare: Presidential Legal Counsel Sergio Apostol 'sneered, "Bring the case to the Supreme Court"' -- apparently calculating that a Supreme Court defeat would damage GMA less than 'a media feast' on Neri's revelations

The doctrinal yardstick: CJP measures the Palace's chances against Philippine jurisprudence, 'especially' Senate v. Ermita (April 20, 2006, by Justice Conchita Carpio Morales), rather than the US cases Dean Raul Pangalangan had analyzed

Parameters 1-2: Congress, 'in aid of legislation,' has a constitutional right to information and officials a duty to provide it (its power of inquiry 'as extensive as the power to legislate'); the President may withhold information only in three categories -- state (military/diplomatic) secrets, informer's privilege, and the 'generic privilege for internal deliberations' (e.g., closed-door Cabinet meetings)

Parameters 3-4: 'disclosure is the rule and secrecy is the exception,' so a claim must show 'the superiority of the public interest' served; and 'only the President' may invoke it personally, or authorize the Executive Secretary to do so 'By order of the President' after personally consulting her

Parameters 5-6: the privilege covers 'categories of information, not of officials' (so it could even shield a waiter who overheard Cabinet secrets); and both the legislative subpoena and any exemption request must state enough detail (the inquiry's nature, possible questions, the facts and reasons for secrecy) for Congress to decide prudently, with the Supreme Court judging any dispute

The verdict and the politics: the Palace had not justified secrecy or followed the process, so its chances were poor; yet earlier inquiries (the 'fertilizer scam' involving Joc-Joc Bolante, the North Rail investigation, the 'Hello Garci' fiasco, the Venable contract) remained 'in limbo,' and the 'Palace strategy' of muddling, delaying and diverting had worked for lack of 'sufficient public outrage' -- 'Kawawa naman tayong mga Pinoy!'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's November 25, 2007 Inquirer column, attacks the Palace's bid to suppress former NEDA chief Romulo Neri's Senate testimony in the $329-million national broadband network (NBN) scandal through a 'nebulous claim of executive privilege.' Neri had testified that resigned Comelec Chair Benjamin Abalos offered him a P200-million bribe ('Sec, may 200 ka dito') but 'clammed up' on President Arroyo's involvement; Presidential Legal Counsel Sergio Apostol then 'sneered, "Bring the case to the Supreme Court,"' apparently calculating that a court loss would damage GMA less than 'a media feast' on Neri's revelations. Measuring the Palace's chances against the parameters set in Senate v. Ermita (2006, by Justice Carpio Morales), CJP lays out a six-point primer on executive privilege: Congress, 'in aid of legislation,' has a right to information and officials a duty to provide it; the President may withhold only three categories (state secrets, informer's privilege, and internal deliberations); 'disclosure is the rule and secrecy is the exception,' requiring a showing of 'the superiority of the public interest'; only the President may invoke it (or the Executive Secretary 'By order of the President'); it covers information, not officials (even 'a waiter' who overheard Cabinet secrets); and both the subpoena and any exemption request must be detailed enough for Congress to judge, with the Supreme Court resolving disputes. On that basis the Palace had not justified secrecy or followed the process, so its chances were poor. But CJP's sharper point is political: earlier inquiries -- the fertilizer scam (Joc-Joc Bolante), North Rail, 'Hello Garci' and the Venable contract -- remained 'in limbo,' and the 'Palace strategy' of muddling issues, delaying resolution and tiptoeing 'from crisis to crisis' had worked because public outrage was never 'enough... to rattle and shoo away GMA.' 'Kawawa naman tayong mga Pinoy!'
